title: EPS-95 pensioners and the higher pension question
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Millions of retired private sector employees live on a small monthly pension. What they ask for.
body:
For millions of retired workers in the organised sector, the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 (EPS-95) is the only regular income in old age. It is run by the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) and pays a monthly pension to workers who have contributed for at least ten years. Two questions have remained at the centre of the pensioners' demands for years: the very low minimum pension, and the slow progress of the "higher pension" option that the Supreme Court allowed in November 2022. This post explains both, with the latest figures that the Government has placed before Parliament, and sets out the position of BMS.

## How the scheme is funded

The way EPS-95 is funded explains much of the argument. A worker's pension is paid from a fund, and the fund is built from contributions. An employer pays 8.33 per cent of the worker's wages into the pension fund, and the Central Government adds 1.16 per cent, on wages up to a monthly ceiling of Rs 15,000. Benefits are paid only from these accumulations. When the ceiling is Rs 15,000, contributions on salary above it do not go into the pension fund unless the worker and employer have opted otherwise, which is why the "higher pension" question exists at all.

## The minimum pension: Rs 1,000

Under the scheme, the minimum pension is Rs 1,000 a month. The Government provides budgetary support to maintain that minimum, but the amount has not been revised for years, while prices of food, medicines and rent have kept rising. Pensioners' organisations have asked for a substantial increase, a minimum of Rs 7,500 being the figure most often mentioned, together with dearness allowance and medical benefits.

The Government's position was restated in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on 1 December 2025. The Minister of State for Labour and Employment, Shobha Karandlaje, said that the Centre was not considering raising the minimum pension from Rs 1,000 to Rs 7,500. She gave no timeline for any revision. The reason she gave was an actuarial deficit: the valuation of the fund as on 31 March 2019 showed that the fund's liabilities were more than its assets, which limits how far benefits can be enhanced. A Member of Parliament also asked in the same session why dearness allowance is not paid to EPS pensioners.

The disagreement is therefore a clear one. Pensioners say that Rs 1,000 a month cannot meet the cost of living. The Government says that the scheme's finances do not allow a large rise. The reader should note that these are two different arguments, one about need and one about money, and a lasting solution has to address both.

## The higher pension judgment

The second question comes from the Supreme Court. On 4 November 2022, the Court, in the case widely cited as EPFO v. Sunil Kumar, upheld the provision under which eligible employees may contribute on their actual salary above the wage ceiling and so qualify for a higher pension, and it set conditions and timelines for the exercise. The EPFO built a process for applications, and employers were asked to verify the details.

The Government's own figures, given in replies to Parliament and reported in December 2025, show both the scale of the exercise and how slow it has been:

- About 17.49 lakh joint option applications had been filed by 11 July 2023.
- Employers had forwarded about 15.24 lakh of these by 31 January 2025.
- The EPFO issued 4,27,308 demand letters, asking applicants to deposit the amount due, and 34,060 cases were later found ineligible, mostly for non-payment of the required contribution.
- About 2,33,303 applicants had paid or given their consent, of whom 96,274 were in service and 1,37,029 were retired.
- 1,24,457 revised Pension Payment Orders had been issued, and 12,572 were awaiting final approval.

The Minister told Parliament that the EPFO had processed nearly 99 per cent of applications. She also said that pensions are calculated on a pro-rata basis under Paragraph 12 of the scheme, a formula that she described as having been upheld by the Supreme Court.

## Why applicants still face difficulty

Several of these numbers help to explain what applicants have been complaining about. Out of lakhs of applications, relatively few have ended with a revised pension order. Applicants have been asked to deposit the amounts shown in demand letters, which have to be worked out over many years of contributions, and understanding how a demand was calculated can be difficult. Pensioners' organisations have described delays and queries in the process, which this post cannot independently verify, while the Government's figures show an exercise that it considers largely complete. The truth is probably that the two pictures describe different stages, and that a worker's case can be "processed" without being finally settled.

## BMS and pensioners

BMS has taken part in the demand for improved pensions. In its memorandum to the Union Labour Minister on 21 November 2025, it asked for the minimum pension to be raised from Rs 1,000 to Rs 7,500, linked to the Consumer Price Index and to the Ayushman Bharat health scheme. In the same memorandum it asked that the EPF wage ceiling be raised from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000, which would increase both contributions and future benefits for lakhs of workers who now fall above the limit. The BMS family also includes a senior citizens' organisation, the Varisht Nagarik Parisangh, and BMS has asked the EPFO to simplify and speed up the higher pension process.

## What would help

- **A published timetable** for the disposal of pending higher pension cases, with clear reasons given when an application is rejected.
- **A plain explanation** of each demand letter, showing how the amount was worked out, so that a pensioner can check it.
- **A review of the minimum pension**, with a stated formula that links it to prices, instead of one fixed number for decades.
- **An honest actuarial discussion** between the Government, employers and workers' representatives about how the fund can be strengthened, since the argument about the deficit cannot be settled without it.
- **Support for workers in small establishments** who find it hard to get employer records for old years.

## What pensioners can do now

A person with a pending application should keep the acknowledgement number, copies of the joint option form and any demand letter, and check the status on the EPFO portal. Where a demand letter seems to be wrong, a written representation to the regional office, with copies of past wage records, is the correct first step, and a copy should be kept.

## Why it matters

Pension is deferred wage. A worker who has served for thirty or forty years has set aside a part of each month's earnings for the day when work stops. A pension of Rs 1,000 a month, or a long wait for a revised pension that was legally allowed, feels like a promise that has not been kept. A society is judged by how it treats those who have retired, and the EPS-95 question will remain on the national agenda until the minimum pension reflects the cost of living and the higher pension process reaches the pensioners it was meant for.
